title: Become an Effective Software Engineering Manager
subtitle: How to Be the Leader Your Development Team Needs

oneLine.text: Management is a separate craft from engineering, built from deliberate everyday habits.

pullQuote.text: Your output is the team’s output. Design your week so the work only you can do gets done.

items.name: Your own time
items.gist: A manager’s calendar fills by default, so attention and a task system have to be designed on purpose.

items.name: One-to-ones
items.gist: Regular private conversations are where trust, feedback and career growth actually happen.

items.name: Delegation
items.gist: Handing over stretching work, with clear expectations, is how people grow and how the manager scales.

items.name: Feedback
items.gist: Timely, specific feedback in both directions keeps small problems small.

items.gist: A structured, consistent process, because who joins shapes the team for years.

sections.body: This is the book I would hand a strong engineer on their first day as a manager. It treats management as a separate craft with its own habits, which is the thing most new managers get wrong, and it is practical enough to use on Monday.

Engineering management is a different job from engineering, not a promotion of it. The manager’s work is to create the conditions in which the team does its best work, and that comes from deliberate, repeatable habits: managing your own time, holding regular one-to-ones, giving feedback, delegating, and hiring well.

- I run one-to-ones as the report’s meeting, not mine: their agenda first, status last, because status belongs in a written update.
- I protect a weekly block for the work only a manager can do: hiring, unblocking, writing down decisions. Everything else can be interrupted.
- With the agent fleet I apply the same idea of delegation: a clear contract in AGENTS.md, a definition of done, and a check that verifies the work instead of me watching it happen.
- When I hand someone a stretch project, I say out loud what “done” looks like and when we will check in. Silence is not delegation.

- If I disappeared for two weeks, which decisions would stall, and why are they still mine?
- Does every person on the team know what is expected of them this quarter, in writing?
- When did each person last get specific feedback, positive or negative?
- Are one-to-ones being cancelled more often than they are held?
- Is our hiring loop the same for every candidate, or does it depend on who is free?

Its core claim, that your output is now the team’s output, is the most important mindset shift in the job. I also agree with its emphasis on systems over heroics: a calendar, a task list and a hiring rubric beat good intentions every time.

It is written for managers of one team in a fairly healthy company. It says less about politics, reorgs, layoffs or leading through a crisis, and a manager in a struggling organization will find its advice assumes more support than they have. Parts of it are also familiar if you have already read The Manager’s Path.

- Management is a different job, not a promotion.
- Design your week, or other people will design it for you.
- One-to-ones are the core habit; protect them.
- Delegation is a development tool, not just a way to offload work.
Read it with **The Manager’s Path**. Stanier teaches the daily craft of running one team; Fournier shows how that craft changes at every level above it.
Skip it if you have managed managers for years; it will mostly confirm what you know. It also misleads if you treat it as complete: it is a starter kit, not a guide to organizational politics.

ideas.title: Your output is the team’s output
ideas.summary: Once you manage, your contribution is measured by what the team achieves, not by what you produce yourself.
ideas.caveat: The feedback loop is slow; new managers often feel unproductive for months and are tempted to retreat into coding.
ideas.example: A new manager who keeps taking the hardest tickets can become the team’s bottleneck instead of its multiplier.

ideas.title: Manage yourself first
ideas.summary: A manager’s calendar fills up by default, so time, attention and a reliable system for tasks have to be managed on purpose.
ideas.caveat: The right system is personal; the point is having one, not copying a particular tool.

ideas.title: One-to-ones are the core habit
ideas.summary: Regular, private conversations with each report are where trust, feedback and career growth happen.
ideas.caveat: They decay into status updates unless the report owns much of the agenda.

ideas.title: Delegate to grow people
ideas.summary: Delegation is a development tool: hand over work that stretches someone, with clear expectations and support.
ideas.caveat: Handing off work without context or backing is abdication, not delegation.

ideas.title: Hiring is high leverage
ideas.summary: Who joins the team shapes it for years, so hiring deserves a structured, consistent process.
ideas.caveat: Structure reduces bias and noise but does not remove them.
